title: Abram lets Lot choose (Genesis 13)
hookLine: to keep the peace, the elder lets his nephew take first pick of the land

lines: TOO MANY SHEEP, NOT ENOUGH GRASS.
cards: Abram comes back from Egypt rich: cattle, silver and gold. His nephew Lot, who came with him, has his own flocks and herds and tents.
And now there's a problem anyone who has shared a small apartment will recognize: there isn't room for both.

The land can't bear them dwelling together, the Torah says, and the herdsmen start to quarrel, Abram's shepherds against Lot's, over grass and water. It could turn into something worse. Abram is the elder.

God promised this land to his offspring, not to Lot. He could tell his nephew where to go. Instead, he does something that would surprise anyone who has ever split a pizza, a bedroom or a family house.

teach.b: Abram says to Lot, in the old JPS translation: "Let there be no strife, I pray thee, between me and thee, and between my herdmen and thy herdmen; for we are brethren."
In Hebrew, anashim achim: we are men who are brothers. Then he points at the whole land. Is it not all before you?
If you go left, I'll go right. If you go right, I'll go left. You choose first.

teach.h: LOT LIFTS HIS EYES TO THE GREEN.
teach.b: So Lot lifts up his eyes. He sees the plain of the Jordan, well watered everywhere, like the garden of the Lord, takes it, and moves his tents toward a city called Sodom.
The Torah adds one quiet, ominous line: the men of Sodom were very wicked. Now notice the eyes. Lot lifted his eyes and chose what looked best.

teach.h: ABRAM LIFTS HIS EYES TO A GIFT.
teach.b: Right after Lot leaves, God speaks to Abram: lift up your eyes, look north and south and east and west. All the land you see, I give to you and your children. Walk through it.

What Abram let go of came back to him as a gift, and bigger. One midrash adds that the fight started because Lot's shepherds let their animals graze in other people's fields, while Abram's kept theirs muzzled.
And the Mishnah gives a name to what Abram does here, though it isn't speaking about this story: Hillel taught, be among the students of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace.
Sometimes that means being the one who says: you choose first.

how: Jews read this story in the Torah portion Lech Lecha; its words "for we are brethren" and Hillel's teaching about loving and pursuing peace are often quoted when family members or neighbors settle a dispute.

o: we're family, so let there be no strife
two brothers who fight over an inheritance
shepherds who share one well and field

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: chose the green plain of the Jordan
God to Abram, after Lot leaves

s: Abram, as the elder, took first pick of the land
he gave the first choice to Lot: if you go left, I'll go right.
Lot's choice moved him toward Sodom
he pitched his tents toward Sodom, and the Torah notes its people were very wicked.
after Lot left, God told Abram to look in every direction
north, south, east and west: all the land you see I give to you.

games.q: you're Abram. your herdsmen and your nephew's are fighting, and God has promised this land to your offspring. what do you do?
o: tell Lot where he can graze.
games.why: he says, let there be no strife, for we are brethren, and offers Lot the first choice. Lot takes the green plain.

practice: Think of one small contest coming up today: who gets the good chair, which show to watch, where to eat, who speaks first in the meeting.
Picture turning to the other person and saying, you choose, and notice how that feels in your body, tight or loose. If you pray, you can ask for a generous heart.

wordCard.voice: Anashim achim, Hebrew for men who are brothers, the reason Abram gave up first choice. The elder, who had every right to pick, gives it away to keep the peace.

orig.note: Hebrew: men who are brothers. Abram's reason for giving up first choice.

carryVoice: Your line: you choose first. For Abram, family came before first pick. That's forty days.

sources.q: Let there be no strife, I pray thee, between me and thee, and between my herdmen and thy herdmen; for we are brethren.
